title: Ambient particulate matter pollution and stroke burden

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Ambient particulate matter pollution and stroke burden》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · section-2-p2】Given the high mortality and disability rates of stroke and its substantial societal burden, and since air pollution is a known risk factor for stroke, with ambient particulate matter pollution (APMP) as a core component and primary concern in air pollution, clarifying the relationship between APMP and stroke occurrence is critical for disease prevention and control.45 A previous study has shown that APMP ranks fourth among the factors influencing the global stroke burden, accounting for 20.2% of the stroke burden in 2019.6 The number of deaths attributed to APMP exceeds 4 million annually.78 Notably, if the air quality in all countries were to meet the guidelines set by the World Health Organization, human life expectancy is expected to increase by more than 14 years, which fully highlights the significant importance of reducing APMP concentrations.9 From 1990 to 2019, the stroke burden attributed to APMP showed an upward trend.10 Meanwhile, reduced precipitation caused by climate change may further exacerbate APMP.11 Therefore, sustained attention and in-depth research on APMP are essential. Utilizing the most recent Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2021 data, this study analyzed the research gap regarding the impact of APMP on stroke burden from 1990 to 2021, assessed the global stroke burden attributable to APMP in air pollution. Further analysis is categorized by age, sex, countries, socio-demographic index (SDI) and GBD regions. Spatial and temporal trends, as well as health inequities across different SDI locations in APMP-related stroke burden, are investigated. This study aims to provide a statistical basis for health professionals and policymakers to implement large-scale actions to reduce stroke burden and socioeconomic costs, offering evidence for precise prevention and control strategies.

【Introduction · section-2-p1】Previous studies have confirmed that among all risk factors for stroke, air pollution is a modifiable one, and reducing air pollution can decrease the incidence of stroke.123 Current hypotheses on the impact of air pollution on stroke include mechanisms such as direct ischemic damage to cerebral vessels or endothelial dysfunction caused by air pollutants, which can trigger cerebral vasospasm and autonomic dysfunction, and even intracranial pressure spikes from pollutant-induced coughing, potentially leading to stroke.4 Although these hypotheses are biologically plausible, most existing studies rely on associations between regional average pollution levels and disease occurrence, lacking comprehensive data to support definitive causal conclusions.

【Statistical analysis · section-6-p4】To assess socioeconomic inequality in stroke burden attributable to APMP, we used the slope index of inequality (SII) and the concentration index (CI). The SII measures absolute differences in rates across the SDI spectrum, while the CI quantifies relative inequality based on the distribution of outcomes by socioeconomic rank. CI values range from –1 to +1, with negative values indicating a higher burden in lower-SDI populations and positive values indicating a concentration in higher-SDI groups. For all indicators, a value of zero reflects perfect equality.

【The trends of ambient particulate matter pollution-related stroke burden by socio-demographic index from 1990 to 2021 · section-17-p1】From 1990 to 2021, the socioeconomic inequality in stroke burden attributable to APMP showed a divergent trend. The SII declined from 9.02 to –155.51, indicating a substantial increase in absolute inequality, with a growing burden among lower-SDI populations. In contrast, the CI decreased slightly from 0.20 to 0.16, suggesting a modest reduction in relative inequality, although the burden remained disproportionately concentrated in higher-SDI regions. This divergence shows the need to interpret absolute and relative inequality measures in parallel when evaluating environmental health disparities (Figure 5).

From 1990 to 2021, the socioeconomic inequality in stroke burden attributable to APMP showed a divergent trend.
